## Nine deploys a day at Meridian Freight, down from one every six weeks

For years, Meridian Freight's platform team shipped on a six-week clock. A single release carried about forty merged branches, so failures were hard to trace. When the January release broke checkout for two hours, the on-call engineer burned most of a day bisecting toward the one bad commit.

"People weren't writing code slowly," says Priya Ramanathan, who leads the team. "Nobody wanted to be the person who broke the release, so everyone waited."

The team put [Platform] on two services in March instead of the whole estate. The mechanical part came first: every merge to main now builds, runs tests, and lands in staging on its own. The harder part was trust. They spent roughly ten weeks writing enough integration coverage to believe the pipeline when it said a change was fine.

Fourteen services now take about nine production deploys a day. Change failure rate fell from 18% to 4%. Median time to restore fell from four hours to eleven minutes, largely because a bad deploy is one commit to inspect rather than forty.

Two services touching customer billing still require a human approval. Ramanathan calls that deliberate and likely permanent.

"What surprised me was how it changed the ideas people bring up," she says. "Cheap shipping means someone will try the small thing. It used to not be worth the ceremony."
